blocks.text: Isaiah 65:17-25 gathers images of renewed Jerusalem, transformed longevity, and a world without harm. Along with Isaiah 25-27, these images became foundational for later Jewish and Christian hope concerning resurrection and new creation.

The phrase “new heavens and a new earth” has been understood in different ways: as transformation, renewal, or replacement. Likewise, “new creation” can be read as referring to a person in Messiah, a changed way of perceiving and relating, or creation’s renewal breaking into the present. The chapter’s language supports the importance of the question, while leaving its precise scope debated.

The Great Isaiah Scroll preserves an almost complete text of Isaiah and is broadly aligned with the Masoretic tradition, though it also contains many spelling and substantive differences. Its witness, along with other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretations, is a reminder to distinguish a passage’s literary sense and historical referent from later readings, quotations, allusions, and broader canonical interpretations.

sections.title: Reading Isaiah in Its Wider Book Context
